title: HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs

paper.title: HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs
paper.abstract:
Abstract Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents.
Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self-improvement (RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution costs.
We introduce HarnessPro , a label-free method for evolving harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost.
In this setting, candidate harnesses are evaluated using LLM-generated tests without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests.
Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with different performance-cost priorities, and implement them as candidate harnesses.
Rather than returning a single harness, HarnessPro uses normalized weighted squared-distance selection to provide cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) harnesses for different deployment budgets.
Selected harnesses enter the next iteration, where execution feedback guides further updates.
Our experiments cover Terminal-Bench 2, SWE-Bench Pro, and ProgramBench, using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code.
Across these benchmarks using GPT-5.5 with Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro achieves an average pass-rate gain of 2.0 percentage points and an average per-task cost reduction of 26.1% relative to RHO.
This advantage also holds when using GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Code is available at this link .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: An agent harness is the software infrastructure that manages interactions between a large language model (LLM) and its environment ( Grace et al., 2026 ) . Recent work on recursive self-improvement (RSI) ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) uses past execution trajectories to diagnose problems and guide harness updates that improve performance on future tasks ( Suzgun et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ; Pan et al., 2026a ) . However, these methods often pursue performance gains through more extensive exploration and stronger verification ( Lin et al., 2026 ; Pan et al., 2026a ) . These efforts improve performance, but often at the cost of higher token consumption and increased latency. This trade-off is less appealing in practical deployment, where the execution cost and latency also matter. We therefore ask: Can recursive harness self-improvement deliver better performance at lower execution cost? Toward this goal, we introduce HarnessPro , a label-free method for recursive harness self-improvement that uses both performance and cost metrics to guide harness updates and candidate selection. It orchestrates several specialized agents to turn execution feedback into successive harness updates. A trajectory analyzer examines repeated rollouts to identify failures and avoidable overhead. Guided by different performance-cost priorities , a planner turns these diagnoses into harness improvement plans, which an editor implements as executable harness candidates. A test-synthesis agent provides fixed tests for evaluating the candidates without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests. Candidates that underperform the initial harness or are Pareto-dominated are discarded. To accommodate different budgets, we then use normalized weighted squared-distance selection ( Marler and Arora, 2004 ) to retain representative harnesses for cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) modes. The selected harnesses then enter the next epoch, where further updates pursue different performance-cost priorities. We evaluate HarnessPro on Terminal-Bench 2 ( The Terminal-Bench Team, 2025 ) , SWE-Bench Pro ( Deng et al., 2026 ) , and ProgramBench ( Yang et al., 2026a ) , using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. With both backbone models, HarnessPro improves task performance while reducing execution cost . For example, on Terminal-Bench 2 with GPT-5.5 and Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro outperforms RHO ( Pan et al., 2026a ) in pass rate by 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean cost per task by 33.9%. For more cost-sensitive deployments, the medium mode delivers performance comparable to RHO at substantially lower execution cost. An analysis of the evolved harnesses shows that HarnessPro does not improve agents simply by compressing context or increasing reasoning effort. The evolved harnesses dynamically allocate reasoning effort and tool budgets based on task descriptions, while runtime hooks steer execution from exploration toward convergence based on the assigned budgets. They also adopt tool-output compression like RTK ( Szymkowiak, 2026 ) and streamline instructions to reduce redundant prompt content, while retaining necessary context and final verification. Together, these mechanisms curb avoidable overhead while preserving the reasoning and verification needed for task success, thereby advancing the performance-cost Pareto frontier. Our contributions are threefold: • We introduce HarnessPro , a multi-agent framework that simultaneously optimizes performance and cost by analyzing execution trajectories and recursively improving harnesses. • We assess candidate artifacts with fixed LLM-generated tests rather than direct LLM judgments, improving failure detection without access to official tests. • Across three benchmarks, HarnessPro improves performance while reducing cost and latency, yielding a series of harnesses with different performance-cost trade-offs.

sections.heading: Agent and harness optimization.
sections.text: Agent optimization has expanded from prompts and pre-defined workflows to the executable harness surrounding a model. AFlow searches graphs of model-invoking operators using execution feedback ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . More recent systems directly modify harness components: agentic harness engineering makes edits traceable ( Lin et al., 2026 ) , HarnessFix diagnoses failures before applying repairs ( Chen et al., 2026a ) , and HarnessX composes harnesses from typed primitives using trajectory evidence ( Chen et al., 2026b ) . RHO uses LLMs to evaluate and compare execution trajectories without ground-truth labels, guiding harness evolution toward higher task success ( Pan et al., 2026a ) . In contrast, our method, HarnessPro , optimizes both task success rate and monetary cost. Rather than returning a single harness, it produces a set of harnesses with different performance-cost trade-offs, organized into lite, medium, and heavy tiers.

sections.heading: Component optimization and inference-time budget allocation.
sections.text: Some methods focus on specific components, such as skills or memory ( Pan et al., 2026b ) . SkillOpt optimizes skill documents ( Yang et al., 2026b ) , while SkillMOO and FRAMES incorporate cost or regression constraints into skill evolution ( Gong et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Dynamic Cheatsheet and ReasoningBank retain reusable strategies from past experience ( Suzgun et al., 2026 ; Ouyang et al., 2026 ) , while Sleep-time Compute builds reusable memory by reasoning over context before a query arrives ( Lin et al., 2025 ) . MemoryCPT jointly optimizes memory construction, retrieval, and summarization ( Lei et al., 2026 ) . Other work addresses budget allocation at inference time: BATS learns a budget-aware policy for allocating model tokens and external tool calls ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , while COMPAS jointly selects models, prompts, and decoding settings according to task difficulty ( Gong et al., 2026b ) . HarnessPro instead uses past trajectories to evolve the entire harness, including instructions, skills, tools, hooks, and verification rules. sections.heading: 3 Problem Setting
sections.text: A harness h ∈ ℋ h\in\mathcal{H} is the software runtime layer that manages a foundation model’s interactions and execution. It includes prompts, tools and skills, context and memory mechanisms, hooks, and verification policies ( Yehudai et al., 2026 ; OpenAI, 2026 ) . Given a task x x , the harness determines what information the agent receives, which actions it can take, and how those actions are executed, directly influencing both task success and resource consumption. An agent equipped with harness h h solves task x x , producing a trajectory τ h ​ ( x ) = Solve ⁡ ( h , x ) \tau_{h}(x)=\operatorname{Solve}(h,x) that records tool calls, environment feedback, and the final artifact. Recursive self-improvement uses trajectories from previous tasks to guide harness evolution and improve performance on future tasks. Below, we define the three evaluation metrics: pass rate, execution cost, and runtime latency.

sections.heading: Pass rate.
sections.text: To prevent test-set leakage, we partition tasks into training, validation, and test sets, denoted by 𝒟 train \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} , 𝒟 val \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}} , and 𝒟 test \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}} . Outcomes on the training set are used to update harnesses, while the validation set is used to evaluate and select candidate harnesses. The test set is used only for final evaluation after evolution. For a task x ∈ 𝒟 test x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}} , the official tests evaluate the final artifact produced by τ h ​ ( x ) \tau_{h}(x) . We set Pass ⁡ ( τ h ​ ( x ) ) = 1 \operatorname{Pass}(\tau_{h}(x))=1 if all official tests pass and Pass ⁡ ( τ h ​ ( x ) ) = 0 \operatorname{Pass}(\tau_{h}(x))=0 otherwise. The pass rate is the fraction of test tasks that pass all official tests, PR ⁡ ( h ) = 1 | 𝒟 test | ​ ∑ x ∈ 𝒟 test Pass ⁡ ( τ h ​ ( x ) ) \mathrm{PR}(h)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}}\operatorname{Pass}\!\left(\tau_{h}(x)\right) .

sections.heading: Cost.
sections.text: We compute execution cost from token usage, distinguishing uncached input, cached input, and output tokens because they are billed at different prices. For each task x x , we aggregate these token counts over all model calls in τ h ​ ( x ) \tau_{h}(x) and compute its cost c h ​ ( x ) c_{h}(x) using the prices in Table 4 (Appendix A ). We report the average cost per test task as C ⁡ ( h ) = 1 | 𝒟 test | ​ ∑ x ∈ 𝒟 test c h ​ ( x ) C(h)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}}c_{h}(x) .

sections.heading: Latency.
sections.text: We define task latency as the wall-clock time from the start of agent execution to its completion: ℓ h ​ ( x ) = T end ​ ( τ h ​ ( x ) ) − T start ​ ( τ h ​ ( x ) ) \ell_{h}(x)=T_{\mathrm{end}}(\tau_{h}(x))-T_{\mathrm{start}}(\tau_{h}(x)) . The time spent grading the final output is not included in task latency. We average task latencies over the test set to obtain the mean latency, L ⁡ ( h ) = 1 | 𝒟 test | ​ ∑ x ∈ 𝒟 test ℓ h ​ ( x ) L(h)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}}\ell_{h}(x) . Because model response times fluctuate with server load and network conditions, we treat latency as an auxiliary metric rather than an optimization objective.

sections.heading: Optimization objective.
sections.text: We aim to evolve harnesses that improve performance while reducing cost. We formulate the optimization problem as min h ∈ ℋ ⁡ ( − PR ⁡ ( h ) , C ⁡ ( h ) ) s.t. PR ⁡ ( h ) ≥ PR ⁡ ( h 0 ) . \min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\left(-\mathrm{PR}(h),\,C(h)\right)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\mathrm{PR}(h)\geq\mathrm{PR}(h_{0}). (1) Here, h 0 h_{0} is the initial harness. We seek the Pareto frontier and select three representative operating points: cost-focused ( lite ), balanced ( medium ), and performance-focused ( heavy ). However, finding these trade-offs poses two challenges. (1) A vast harness search space. A harness comprises components such as instructions, tools, skills, hooks, and rules, all of which can be modified during evolution. Their possible combinations create a vast, discrete search space that cannot be optimized using gradients. (2) Balancing performance and cost. Additional reasoning, exploration, or verification can improve performance but also consumes more tokens, increasing cost. Conversely, indiscriminately reducing these activities may hurt performance. Advancing the Pareto frontier thus requires analyzing execution trajectories alongside task outcomes and token usage to distinguish necessary computation from avoidable overhead and find the “sweet spot” that reduces cost without compromising performance.

sections.heading: 4 HarnessPro
sections.text: Figure 1: Overview of HarnessPro . In each epoch, it analyzes rollout trajectories, generates candidate harnesses, and selects representatives based on performance and cost. To address these challenges, we introduce HarnessPro , a multi-agent framework that analyzes execution trajectories and iteratively modifies harnesses to advance the performance-cost Pareto frontier. We first outline the evolution process, then describe trajectory-based diagnosis and candidate generation, followed by test-based evaluation and selection.

sections.heading: 4.1 Overview
sections.text:
To keep trajectory collection and analysis manageable, we begin by selecting a training coreset 𝒟 train \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} . Following RHO ( Pan et al., 2026a ) , we use the Determinantal Point Process (DPP) kernel ( Kulesza and Taskar, 2012 ) to balance task difficulty and diversity (Appendix A.1 ). Starting from an executable harness h 0 h_{0} , we maintain a candidate set 𝒜 t \mathcal{A}_{t} of harnesses at epoch t t , initialized as 𝒜 0 = { h 0 } \mathcal{A}_{0}=\{h_{0}\} . In each epoch, HarnessPro employs a multi-agent framework to analyze trajectories of these candidate harnesses on the coreset 𝒟 train \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} to identify task failures, unproductive exploration, and redundant computation. The framework then plans and implements harness modifications to address these issues, producing new executable candidate harnesses as described in Section 4.2 . We evolve harnesses in a label-free setting, without access to ground-truth solutions, official test cases, or graders. Instead of using an LLM to assess and compare trajectories directly, as in RHO ( Pan et al., 2026a ) , we use it to generate tests from task descriptions and trajectories produced by the initial harness. In each epoch, we evaluate candidate harnesses on the validation set using the generated tests, measuring pass rate and execution cost . After discarding candidates that fall below the performance floor or are Pareto-dominated, we use normalized weighted squared-distance selection to retain representatives for cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) modes. The selected harnesses form the candidate set for the next epoch. This process repeats until the epoch limit is reached, after which we fix the harnesses and evaluate them on the test set. sections.text: At epoch t t , we run each harness in the current candidate set 𝒜 t = { h i t } i = 1 | 𝒜 t | \mathcal{A}_{t}=\{h_{i}^{t}\}_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{A}_{t}|} independently G G times on every training task x ∈ 𝒟 train x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} . For candidate harness h ∈ 𝒜 t h\in\mathcal{A}_{t} , this rollout process yields a trajectory τ h t , g ​ ( x ) \tau_{h}^{t,g}(x) and a metric vector m h t , g ​ ( x ) = ( Pass h t , g ⁡ ( x ) , c h t , g ​ ( x ) , ℓ h t , g ​ ( x ) ) m_{h}^{t,g}(x)=\left(\operatorname{Pass}_{h}^{t,g}(x),\ c_{h}^{t,g}(x),\ \ell_{h}^{t,g}(x)\right) . Here, Pass h t , g ⁡ ( x ) \operatorname{Pass}_{h}^{t,g}(x) is 1 if the artifact produced in τ h t , g ​ ( x ) \tau_{h}^{t,g}(x) passes all generated tests in 𝒮 ⁡ ( x ) \mathcal{S}(x) , while c h t , g ​ ( x ) c_{h}^{t,g}(x) and ℓ h t , g ​ ( x ) \ell_{h}^{t,g}(x) record its execution cost and latency. We also retain token usage and tool-call details for later diagnosis. These trajectories and artifacts guide harness self-improvement through a multi-agent framework comprising a trajectory analyzer , an evolution planner , a harness editor , and a test synthesizer . We describe each agent below.

sections.heading: Trajectory Analyzer.
sections.text: Execution trajectories can reveal harness weaknesses, but the relevant evidence is often dispersed across long sequences of model responses and tool outputs, making these weaknesses difficult to locate and interpret. We therefore implement a trajectory-analysis agent to diagnose these problems for each candidate h h and task x x at epoch t t . To reduce the impact of randomness, the agent jointly examines the trajectories { τ h t , g ​ ( x ) } g = 1 G \{\tau_{h}^{t,g}(x)\}_{g=1}^{G} from G G independent rollouts and their metrics { m h t , g ​ ( x ) } g = 1 G \{m_{h}^{t,g}(x)\}_{g=1}^{G} , rather than relying on a single attempt: z ⁡ ( h , x ) = Analyzer ⁡ ( x , { ( τ h t , g ​ ( x ) , m h t , g ​ ( x ) ) } g = 1 G ) . z(h,x)=\operatorname{Analyzer}\!\left(x,\left\{\left(\tau_{h}^{t,g}(x),m_{h}^{t,g}(x)\right)\right\}_{g=1}^{G}\right). (2) The analyzer’s output z ⁡ ( h , x ) z(h,x) reports (1) identified problems, (2) their impact on performance and cost, and (3) their sources and supporting evidence. The evidence includes a concise trajectory summary or relevant excerpts, together with the path of the trajectory file and the relevant event range. Two examples are provided in Appendix C.1 . We combine diagnoses across different tasks as 𝐳 ⁡ ( h ) = ⋃ x ∈ 𝒟 train z ⁡ ( h , x ) \mathbf{z}(h)=\bigcup\nolimits_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}}z(h,x) . If 𝐳 ⁡ ( h ) \mathbf{z}(h) exceeds 64K tokens, the analyzer summarizes it. We similarly collect the metric vectors across training tasks as 𝐦 ⁡ ( h ) = ⋃ x ∈ 𝒟 train { m h t , g ​ ( x ) } g = 1 G \mathbf{m}(h)=\bigcup\nolimits_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}}\{m_{h}^{t,g}(x)\}_{g=1}^{G} . sections.heading: Test Synthesizer.
sections.text: During harness evolution, we follow RHO ( Pan et al., 2026a ) , adopting a label-free setting without access to ground-truth solutions, official tests, or grader feedback. RHO relies on LLM self-preference to select harnesses. However, we find that LLM judges tend to be overly optimistic when assessing the execution trajectories, often treating flawed implementations as successful. We therefore introduce a dedicated test-synthesis agent to generate test cases for evaluation; its instruction, skill, and validation tool are outlined in Appendix C.3 . sections.heading: Data and implementation.
sections.text: We evaluate HarnessPro on Terminal-Bench 2 ( The Terminal-Bench Team, 2025 ) , SWE-Bench Pro ( Deng et al., 2026 ) , and ProgramBench ( Yang et al., 2026a ) , covering terminal tasks, repository-level issue resolution, and program reconstruction. Following the dataset splitting protocol of RHO ( Pan et al., 2026a ) , we hold out 59, 100, and 100 tasks, respectively, for testing. From the remaining tasks in each benchmark, we select a 10-task training set 𝒟 train \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} using the DPP-based coreset selection method ( Kulesza and Taskar, 2012 ) described in Section 4.1 . The remaining tasks form the validation set. We pair GPT-5.5 with Codex 0.147.0 and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code 2.1.231 . Each candidate harness produces G = 3 G=3 rollouts per training task in each epoch. Evolution runs for three epochs on Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-Bench Pro, and four on ProgramBench, retaining up to three harnesses after each epoch. All methods use the same data splits and grading settings. Further implementation details are in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare HarnessPro against several strong harness optimization methods. The original Codex or Claude Code harness is Vanilla , the starting point for optimization. Dynamic Cheatsheet ( Suzgun et al., 2026 ) maintains reusable strategies and code snippets, ReasoningBank ( Ouyang et al., 2026 ) retrieves strategies distilled from past trajectories, and Sleep-time Compute ( Lin et al., 2025 ) prepares reusable memory before new tasks. RHO ( Pan et al., 2026a ) revises harness components through trajectory analysis and selects candidates using LLM self-preference. To separate the effects of cost-aware and recursive optimization, we include two RHO variants. Balance changes only RHO’s optimization instruction, asking for better task performance at lower cost. RHO+Iteration runs Balance for the same number of epochs as HarnessPro . Each subsequent epoch starts from the harness selected in the preceding epoch by the best-of- N N procedure of RHO.

sections.heading: Evaluation metrics.
sections.text: On Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-Bench Pro, a task passes only if all its official tests pass. For ProgramBench, we follow its official evaluation protocol ( Yang et al., 2026a ) and report pass rate as the macro-average of the fraction of test cases passed for each task. We also report mean cost C ⁡ ( h ) C(h) and latency L ⁡ ( h ) L(h) . For HarnessPro , all metrics are given as mean ± \pm sample standard deviation over three runs on Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-Bench Pro, and two on ProgramBench. The token prices used to calculate cost are listed in Table 4 in the appendix.

With GPT-5.5 and Codex, RHO improves performance over Vanilla on all three benchmarks, but also increases execution cost. On SWE-Bench Pro, for example, its mean cost per task rises by 42.6%, from $1.88 to $2.68. For example, on SWE-Bench Pro, our heavy mode reduces mean latency from RHO’s 520 to 412 seconds.

sections.heading: 5.3 Analysis of Evolved Harnesses
sections.text: To understand how HarnessPro improves the performance-cost trade-off, we inspect its evolved harnesses. On Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-Bench Pro, they select an execution profile from each task description. Each profile specifies a reasoning effort level and a tool-call budget. The lite, medium, and heavy modes use different rubrics for profile selection. Runtime hooks enforce the selected budget. For example, on Terminal-Bench 2, when HarnessPro -Medium selects the standard profile, the hooks remind the agent to produce parallel tool calls and avoid redundant checks after 14 tool calls, focus on completing and verifying the task after 26, and block further calls after 44. The reminders are appended to tool results, preserving the prompt prefix for cache reuse. Alongside these dynamic mechanisms, the evolved harnesses also reduce static context redundancy . On Terminal-Bench 2, for instance, tool-output compression like RTK ( Szymkowiak, 2026 ) folds repeated logs and condenses long outputs, while streamlined developer instructions reduce redundant input. This combination curbs recurring prompt overhead and limits the context growth caused by verbose tool feedback, thereby reducing execution cost and latency. Implementation details of these harnesses are in Appendix D.1 .

sections.text: Figure 4 tracks test-set performance and cost across epochs. Across all three benchmarks, HarnessPro advances the performance-cost Pareto frontier through recursive harness self-improvement. On Terminal-Bench 2, each round of evolution improves the retained Pareto frontier , yielding higher pass rates at lower costs. For example, the pass rate of the heavy mode rises from 74.6% in epoch 1 to a mean of 80.8% in epoch 3, while mean cost per task falls from $0.91 to $0.72 . The lite and medium modes also maintain their pass rates from epoch 2 to 3, while their mean costs fall from $0.61 to $0.43 and from $0.68 to $0.56, respectively. The benefits of additional evolution epochs are particularly clear on SWE-Bench Pro, where a single run may raise pass rate at the expense of higher cost . In the medium mode, pass rate rises from 70.0% in epoch 1 to 77.0% in epoch 2, but mean cost also rises from $1.57 to $1.66. Only in epoch 3 does it improve both metrics, with pass rate rising to 79.0% and mean cost falling to $1.26 per task. On ProgramBench, the fourth epoch likewise lowers costs across all three modes while maintaining similar pass rates. These patterns highlight an advantage of recursive self-improvement over single-round evolution. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced HarnessPro , a label-free approach to recursive harness self-improvement that improves task performance while reducing execution cost. To this end, it coordinates trajectory diagnosis and harness modification through a multi-agent framework, with a dedicated planner proposing update plans and LLM-generated tests guiding candidate evaluation. Rather than producing a single harness, HarnessPro offers cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) alternatives to meet different deployment budgets. Experiments across three benchmarks show that HarnessPro can improve task performance while reducing execution cost , with additional benefits in latency . Further analysis attributes these gains to the synergy of multiple evolved mechanisms and shows sustained progress through recursive self-improvement. These findings show that performance and efficiency can improve together, making cost-aware evolution a promising direction for practical recursive self-improvement in harness optimization.

sections.heading: AI Use Statement
sections.text: Generative AI tools were used to assist with software implementation and the drafting and editing of this manuscript. Separately, LLMs are integral to the method studied in this work: they analyze execution trajectories, propose and implement harness updates, and synthesize tests during harness evolution. All AI-assisted code and text were manually reviewed, and all reported results were checked by the authors.

sections.heading: Reasoning effort and mode weights.
sections.text: The default reasoning effort for GPT-5.5 is high on all three benchmarks. For GLM-5.2, the default is max on Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-Bench Pro, but high on ProgramBench, where max tends to induce extensive reasoning and tool use, substantially lengthening execution. For the selection rule in Equation 9 , the performance-cost weights ( α m , β m ) (\alpha_{m},\beta_{m}) are ( 1 , 2 ) (1,2) for lite, ( 1 , 1 ) (1,1) for medium, and ( 2 , 1 ) (2,1) for heavy. These weights remain fixed across epochs.

sections.heading: Generation settings.
sections.text: Our Codex configurations use the Responses API without explicitly setting temperature, top_p, or max_output_tokens. When used through Codex, GPT-5.5 therefore uses its default sampling settings. The model supports up to 128,000 output tokens per response. 2 2 2 https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.5 For GLM-5.2, Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-Bench Pro use temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, and a per-request max_tokens of 131,072. On ProgramBench, GLM-5.2 runtime uses temperature 1.0, top-p 1.0, and max_tokens of 32,000, with a 2,000-turn limit.

sections.heading: Solver and grading budgets.
sections.text: On Terminal-Bench 2, GPT-5.5 uses each task’s native solver limit (600–3,600 seconds on the test set). On SWE-Bench Pro, the solver time limit is 1200 seconds for GPT-5.5 and 7,200 for GLM-5.2, and the grader limit is 3,600 seconds for both models. On ProgramBench, the solver budget is 7,200 seconds, separate from the 14,400 second outer limit for each grading branch. These wall-clock limits are distinct from harness-level tool-call budgets.

sections.heading: Task environments.
sections.text: Terminal-Bench 2 and ProgramBench allocate 8 CPUs and 32 GiB of memory per solver. SWE-Bench Pro runs solvers in host workspaces without an explicit per-task CPU or memory limit. Candidate evaluation uses one rollout per validation task, and final testing is performed only after evolution. Infrastructure failures are excluded and retried to avoid inaccurate results.

sections.heading: Appendix B Evolution Instructions
sections.text: ⬇ Prioritize reducing average execution cost while preserving task correctness and reliable completion . Seek genuine efficiency gains , not lower bills obtained by skipping required work , abandoning difficult tasks , or weakening validation . Use the diagnostics , trajectories , and candidate implementations to distinguish necessary work from avoidable expense . Look for recurring sources of redundant exploration , repeated context , or low - value verification . Consider the total cost of execution , including unsuccessful attempts and any overhead introduced by the proposed change ; fewer steps or shorter outputs alone do not establish an improvement . Possible directions include adapting reasoning effort to individual public tasks , managing context and tool feedback economically , and improving convergence or recovery . Preserve the information and checks needed for dependable results . These are optional search directions , not a checklist : derive any mechanism from the available evidence , without assuming a routing rubric , fixed thresholds , profile taxonomy , or per - task rules . Propose a focused , generalizable plan rather than accumulating optimizations . Explain which observed expense each change addresses , why correctness should be preserved , and what regression risks remain . Distinguish expected savings from measured results ; the fixed external evaluator , not the plan ’ s claims , determines whether quality is maintained and cost is reduced . ⬇ Seek a balanced improvement in task reliability and average execution cost . Treat correctness and efficiency as joint objectives : do not pursue savings by neglecting required behavior , or assume that additional computation necessarily improves quality . A balanced plan should improve the trade - off , not simply average the other directions . Use the diagnostics , trajectories , and candidate implementations to identify where effort contributes to successful completion and where it is redundant . Compare peer candidates to understand their strengths , weaknesses , and interactions , rather than copying their mechanisms wholesale . Prefer changes that remove low - value work while preserving or strengthening the reasoning and validation that matter . Possible directions include task - adaptive reasoning effort , concise but recoverable context , effective use of tool feedback , and verification or recovery guided by observed uncertainty . These are optional hypotheses , not prescribed designs . Infer an appropriate approach from the evidence ; no routing rubric , fixed thresholds , profile names , or per - task rules are supplied . Account for the overhead and complexity of combining changes . Propose a coherent , generalizable plan and explain its expected quality and cost effects together . Make uncertain trade - offs and regression risks explicit , including why any added work is worthwhile . Keep predicted benefits separate from established findings and let the fixed external evaluator determine whether the joint improvement is real . ⬇ Prioritize improving task success while continuing to eliminate avoidable expense . Focus on reliable completion and correct behavior , not more elaborate execution for its own sake . Performance - focused evolution should invest effort where it can address meaningful failures , rather than increase computation uniformly across tasks . Use the diagnostics , trajectories , and candidate implementations to identify consequential failure patterns and the limitations behind them . Examine both successful and unsuccessful executions to distinguish useful reasoning or validation from activity that merely adds cost . Draw on peer candidates when their behavior provides relevant evidence , but do not assume that a more complex harness is a more capable one . Possible directions include adapting reasoning effort to the public task , selective deeper investigation or independent verification , and stronger context or recovery management . These are optional hypotheses , not an implementation recipe . Derive the actual design from evidence ; no routing rubric , fixed thresholds , mandatory review schedule , or per - task rules are supplied . Preserve efficient behavior where additional work has no demonstrated purpose . Propose a focused , generalizable plan that explains which failures it aims to prevent and why the changes should help . If additional work is necessary , state the expected quality benefit , cost implications , and remaining risks without presenting predictions as measured gains . The fixed external evaluator determines whether the improvement justifies the resulting quality - cost trade - off .

sections.heading: Caffe–CIFAR-10.
sections.text: All three runs failed before training. The analyzer separates a shared build bottleneck from run-specific stalls and a potential downstream risk. ⬇ Task : Build CPU - only Caffe and train CIFAR -10 for 500 iterations . Outcome : No run completed conversion or training , saved a model or log , or verified accuracy . Issue 1: All three workflows ended before training . Problem : Run 0 was fixing a protobuf build issue ; run 1 had built Caffe but was downloading CIFAR -10; run 2 was still rebuilding after an out - of - memory ( OOM ) failure . Cost impact : Long installs , builds , and downloads produced no final training artifacts . Evidence : run -0- trace -0. jsonl :89-97; run -1- trace -0. jsonl :96-111; run -2- trace -0. jsonl :74-80. Issue 2: High build parallelism caused OOM failures in every run . Problem : Runs 0 and 1 used make all - j$ ( nproc ), and run 2 used cmake – build build – parallel 7. OOM - killed compiler processes prompted lower - parallelism retries . Quality impact : Runs 0 and 2 still lacked a successful build at the trace end , delaying data preparation and training . Cost impact : Failed compile passes and rebuilds wasted time . Evidence : run -0- trace -0. jsonl :71-89; run -1- trace -0. jsonl :90-96; run -2- trace -0. jsonl :61-80. Issue 3: The most advanced run stalled on the CIFAR -10 download . Problem : Run 1 interrupted a slow single - stream download , installed aria2 , and ended while its replacement parallel download was ongoing . Quality impact : Conversion , mean generation , training , and model verification were not reached despite a completed Caffe build . Cost impact : The interrupted download , package install , and retry added post - build time without completing data preparation . Evidence : run -1- trace -0. jsonl :96-111. Issue 4: A likely downstream data - preparation blocker ( not observed ). Problem : Run 0 configured Caffe without OpenCV , although the stock CIFAR pipeline calls compute_image_mean , which requires USE_OPENCV . Quality impact : Had run 0 reached this step , mean generation would likely have failed ; the trace does not show such a failure . Cost impact : An OpenCV - enabled rebuild or alternative preparation path would likely have been needed after the existing build work . Evidence : run -0- trace -0. jsonl :60-69; run -1- trace -0. jsonl :69; run -2- trace -0. jsonl :36-37. Issue 5: Run 0 recovered from an incorrect source tag . It tried the nonexistent 1.0.0 branch , inspected tags , then used 1.0; this added commands before the build but no lasting quality loss . Evidence : run -0- trace -0. jsonl :27-42.

Outcome : All three rollouts passed the generated tests . Issue 1: Exploration went well beyond the relevant configuration . Problem : All runs dumped large Mailman / Postfix configs and package source / tests after the task and eval narrowed the relevant surface to mailman . cfg , Postfix local delivery , and Mailman LMTP maps . Cost impact : Trace totals reached 1,058,946, 1,763,487, and 2,517,861 input tokens in runs 0, 1, and 2, respectively ; broad dumps and repeated exploration were major contributors . Evidence : run -0- trace -0. jsonl :36-69,86-93,180; run -1- trace -0. jsonl :22-27,175; run -2- trace -0. jsonl :18-19,180. Issue 2: Final evaluations repeated already covered behavior . Problem : Manual join / post / leave smoke tests usefully checked delivery and leave confirmation , but / app / eval . py was rerun after these and earlier evaluations had passed . Quality impact : Extra evals added little end - to - end coverage . Cost impact : Each eval created Unix users , exercised mail queues , and included retry sleeps . Evidence : run -0- trace -0. jsonl :149-153; run -1- trace -0. jsonl :158-173; run -2- trace -0. jsonl :102-122,167-170. Issue 3: Run 2’ s smoke test temporarily broke mail delivery . Problem : Opening / var / mail /< user > with mailbox . mbox () before Postfix created it produced a root - owned mailbox , so confirmation mail bounced . Quality impact : The agent diagnosed this test - induced failure and reran the smoke test successfully ; the final outcome was unaffected . Quality impact : Services ran , so the final result was unaffected . Cost impact : The agent polled , inspected logs and processes , then terminated the wrapper before evaluation . Invalid local recipients might be accepted at SMTP time and fail later , a risk not observed in the tests . Cost impact : Two failed evals and map debugging preceded the fallback . sections.heading: C.3 Test Synthesizer Configuration
sections.text: Our test-synthesis agent uses an instruction and skill together with an MCP-based validation tool. The first two listings present selected passages from the deployed text, with output-schema fields condensed; the third summarizes the tool interface. Together, they show how the agent designs tests from public evidence, checks them against a frozen artifact, and reviews the suite without access to official tests or labels. ⬇ Use $empty - test - authoring . In this one Codex invocation , write ten distinct executable cases , validate them on the frozen Empty product , inspect the results , and self - review the final suite . No separate reviewer is part of this run . ## Evidence boundary Read / work / public - task . json , relevant / public_inputs , and the read - only / empty_product . The task description and public files define the contract ; Empty is only an implementation and execution - diagnostic context , never an answer key . Public sample programs and evaluation helpers may be used . … Do not seek or use the target ’ s hidden official tests , grader , solution , grades , or earlier target suites , locally or online . Do not modify Empty . ## Test design Inventory the public requirements and the actual input and output interfaces before testing Empty . Cover distinct documented behaviors , valid alternatives , boundaries , and justified combinations ; do not invent extra obligations to fill the fixed count . … For each central requirement , invoke the real delivered product and assert a meaningful relation between its output and independent public evidence . A file existing , successful process , shape , nonempty value , or plausible range alone does not establish the required behavior . … Choose the strongest justified oracle available : compatible public reference , known answer , necessary content property , or discriminating metamorphic relation . Never derive expected constants , hashes , tolerated values , or execution paths from Empty . ## Execute and self - review Write the complete suite , then call validate_generated_tests on it . After every executable edit , rerun the tool ; the final executable files must match a completed execution without infrastructure error . Run tests serially . Self - review every case , expected value , and shared helper after the final run . … ## Output contract Write UTF -8 files under / work / output , at most 1 MiB per file and 4 MiB total : - test_generated . py : exactly test_case_0001 through test_case_0010 as unittest . TestCase methods ; no skipped or unconditional padding cases . - case_manifest . json : expected_count : 10; each case has a meaningful description and kind behavioral , format , or unavailable_oracle . - coverage . json : public evidence , requirements mapped to case IDs , checks performed , what was not checked , and limitations . - repair - log . json : demonstrated defects , public evidence , edits , and rerun outcomes ; use [] if no repair was needed . - self - review . json : per - case assessment , reason , public evidence , suggested repair , and any essential or supplemental coverage gaps . ⬇ Read / work / public - task . json and relevant / public_inputs first . Inspect / empty_product only to understand the frozen candidate ’ s interfaces or to diagnose execution . Its files correspond to original paths such as / app , but the snapshot is not an oracle . The available public dependencies and fixture mounts are listed in validation_environment in the task JSON . Disjoint examples are read - only under / examples . Write the suite in / work / output . If MCP discovery fails , send a JSON - RPC tools / call request to python3 / opt / harnesspro / empty - tools / tools / mcp_server . py on stdin . Keep tests and validation calls serial . The model has no Docker socket or official grader . Interpret status = ok , passed = false as a completed execution , not a request to make Empty pass . Treat infra_error as unresolved until its cause is identified . Repair only test defects supported by public evidence , record the change in repair - log . json , and rerun the changed suite . Preserve valid product failures and report any unresolved oracle or setup problem . Review the final test design in the same invocation ; do not launch another reviewer . Public reference tools , if needed , are available in the authoring image ; version manifests are under / opt / harnesspro / reference - tools . sections.heading: D.1.1 Medium Mode
sections.text: The medium mode uses GPT-5.5 throughout, with five execution profiles spanning low, medium, and high reasoning effort. The listings below present its instructions, routing rubric, runtime hooks, and policy settings. ⬇ You are Codex , a non - interactive software agent . Work autonomously until the user ’ s task is complete . Follow the task ’ s integrity , safety , path , and output requirements exactly . Use the available tools to inspect , edit , execute , and verify ; batch independent checks and avoid repeating unchanged reads . Preserve unrelated files and avoid destructive operations outside the requested scope . Do not replace a requested implementation or service with a mock , proxy , or look - alike unless the task explicitly permits that substitution . Do not spawn other agents or ask the user to perform routine steps . Keep progress messages brief . Before finishing , leave every requested artifact at its exact path and run the strongest allowed task - shaped verification . Report the outcome concisely , including any genuine remaining uncertainty . ⬇ Harness guidance is already loaded ; do not inventory harness /. Extract exact artifacts , paths , behavior , integrity restrictions , public interfaces , and final state from task / prompt . md . Use its host - to - container pattern . For black - box work use only public interfaces and implement general behavior . When the task names an API , wrapper , package , revision , runtime , or service , exercise that named interface first and do not silently replace it with a lower - level dependency , mock , proxy , or look - alike behavior ; inspect the public signature or implementation after an interface error . A source - only or single - artifact deliverable should not acquire undeclared runtime helpers . Start with the smallest discriminating probe and batch independent checks . Bound downloads , external interaction , and potentially blocking commands well below the task watchdog ; reserve time for final repair and verification . Validate requested behavior , not only superficial readiness signals . Run mutating workflow checks on disposable fixtures when possible ; if the user is meant to perform the same workflow later , do not leave test data or state that collides with its documented preconditions . Preserve the real requested implementation and durable service state while removing only temporary verification artifacts . For quantitative work , identify units , variables , invariants , and the comparison objective before optimizing ; exercise every publicly stated correctness dimension using a direct reference or invariant when one can be constructed . Keep temporary verification artifacts separate from final deliverables . Before finishing , compare exact contents and state with every explicit requirement . Avoid narration and unchanged rereads ; do not skip necessary validation . ⬇ Choose exactly one profile from observable task characteristics . Optimize expected success per dollar . Never use historical outcomes remembered from prior runs or evaluations . Profiles : - ‘ compact ’: low reasoning ; converge near 4 tool calls and stop near 8. - ‘ lean ’: low reasoning ; converge near 10 calls and stop near 16. - ‘ standard ’: medium reasoning ; converge near 26 calls and stop near 38. - ‘ deep ’: high reasoning ; converge near 30 calls and stop near 48. - ‘ research ’: high reasoning with about 40 calls for source reconstruction . Evidence rules - Use only validation , interaction , dependencies , artifacts , and constraints explicitly described in the task text . Never assume hidden - test behavior , previous attempts , tool output , runtime results , or historical scores . - An undescribed validator has unknown quality , not weak quality . Unknown decisive evidence defaults to ‘ standard ’; missing information alone cannot justify another profile . - A strong oracle must be explicitly local and repeatable and provide localized failure , quantitative error , candidate ranking , deterministic simulation , or a directly inspectable target . Compilation , launch , an open port , one end - to - end request , or whole - task pass / fail is weak only when the text explicitly limits feedback to that undifferentiated signal . - Count distinct evidence - resolvable hypotheses , not files , prose , commands , or retries . Extra iterations are valuable only when described probes can distinguish hypotheses and change the plan . - Include the stated watchdog and expected probe cost in the value of iteration . A precise oracle is not useful enough for ‘ deep ’ when only a few full evaluations can fit and high reasoning does not create more evidence . Apply the following gates in order and stop at the first match . Gate 1: ‘ compact ’ Choose ‘ compact ’ only when low marginal value is explicit and no faithful decomposable oracle is described or structurally possible : 1. Long serial graphical , remote , virtualized , or manual interaction whose correctness depends on visual or hidden state . 2. Unavailable accounts , devices , services , credentials , or changing external state without a faithful local substitute . 3. Broad hidden or effectively unbounded behavior plus exact preservation of unrelated details , with explicitly end - to - end accept / reject feedback . 4. One unchanged artifact must satisfy independent grammars , parsers , runtimes , or environments , while checks expose only a joint accept / reject objective . 5. Bulk media or visual interpretation with no described numerical comparator and correctness resting on visual judgment . Difficulty , visualization , specialization , or virtualization alone is not enough . A small fixed visual artifact , scripted headless setup with direct checks , or local scorer that distinguishes candidates should continue to later gates . File - existence or format checks do not make long visual / media search a strong oracle when the decisive event must still be found by inspecting many frames . Gate 2: ‘ research ’ Choose ‘ research ’ only when the primary deliverable is factual reconstruction requiring multiple accessible sources , version / date alignment , provenance , or a historical snapshot . A multi - record date / version ranking qualifies ; one lookup or research used only to build an artifact does not . If decisive sources are explicitly inaccessible , choose ‘ compact ’. Gate 3: ‘ deep ’ Choose ‘ deep ’ only when a strong local oracle is explicitly described or can be constructed from an exact deterministic reference , transformation , simulator , or runtime supplied by the task , and at least one shape applies : 1. Latent structure or parameter recovery plus exact compatibility or a quantitative objective . 2. Correctness spans several interacting components , stages , or states and can be checked through exact invariants , reference behavior , or round trips . 3. Damaged structured - state recovery requiring competing format , ordering , or transformation hypotheses . 4. Constrained synthesis , compression , size reduction , or candidate search with coupled hard constraints and an executable scorer . 5. Nontrivial recovery , inference , or attack derived from many observations with exact candidate validation . 6. An inverse problem with a deterministic simulator or quantitative objective . 7. Candidate construction against a deterministic transformation or runtime , with multiple materially different mechanisms that can be executed and observed . 8. A severely constrained reimplementation of deterministic reference behavior , where exact candidate outputs can be compared locally despite language , size , compatibility , or dependency restrictions . 9. One source artifact must implement behavior while remaining valid under two or more independent grammars , compilers , or runtimes , each of which can be exercised separately for localized feedback . Do not choose ‘ deep ’ for terminology , long specifications , ordinary security or reverse engineering , or hidden tests alone . Ordinary performance tuning and ordinary state propagation through services , hooks , or deployments are ‘ standard ’. A binary validator alone is insufficient , but a deterministic local transformation plus executable behavior can support meaningful candidate iteration even when the final verdict is binary . Prefer ‘ standard ’ when each candidate evaluation is described as expensive enough to consume a material part of the watchdog and the work is mainly bounded tuning against one supplied evaluator . Modifying an existing artifact against one supplied evaluator remains ‘ standard ’ merely because it combines a quantitative objective with preservation constraints ; ‘ deep ’ additionally requires latent recovery , combinatorial search , or several materially different candidate mechanisms . ‘ deep ’ requires room for several evidence - changing iterations . Gate 4: ‘ lean ’ Choose ‘ lean ’ only when all are explicit : 1. Bounded , mostly deterministic work . 2. At most two meaningful uncertainties . 3. A credible plan before broad exploration . 4. A direct local check covering nearly all decisive behavior . 5. About eight or fewer evidence - producing calls for inspection , implementation , and final validation . Typical cases are a localized transformation ; enumerable mechanical cleanup with a deterministic final scan ; a simple build or single - service setup with one main uncertainty and a direct test ; or bounded numerical work with direct value , shape , or residual validation . Do not choose ‘ lean ’ when several coupled uncertainties require iterative candidate comparison , or when recovering latent state requires materially different hypotheses . Apply the ‘ deep ’ gate first when a constructible exact or quantitative reference makes those iterations useful . Also do not choose ‘ lean ’ for broad cleanup where unaffected content must be preserved exactly and the set of true matches is not explicitly bounded ; false - positive scope is a separate uncertainty even when a final scan is deterministic . Use ‘ standard ’ when coordinating several schemas , formats , subsystems , integration boundaries , correctness / performance constraints , or hidden edge - case families . Also use it for multi - service state propagation , broad security properties , builds combining source provenance with feature exclusion and multiple runtime modes , corpus - wide cleanup with exact preservation of unaffected content , or unstructured recovery with several evidence paths but only final candidate checks . Gate 5: ‘ standard ’ Choose ‘ standard ’ for everything else , including unknown oracle quality . It is the default for ordinary implementation , debugging , data processing , service setup , bounded numerical work , and analysis with several actionable uncertainties , and should normally be the plurality . sections.heading: D.3 ProgramBench
sections.text: The ProgramBench medium-mode harness uses a fixed GPT-5.5 high-effort profile instead of task-adaptive routing. The workflow builds an independent program from bundled documentation and permitted black-box probes, validates it against the public reference, and reserves time for a clean offline rebuild. Listing shows the stored harness files. This fixed-profile harness has no routing rubric. The evaluator configures Codex to load the instruction file and execute the budget hook. ⬇ README . md runtime / model_instructions . md policy . json hook . py ⬇ # ProgramBench Reconstruction Harness Use this harness as a task - agnostic control loop for rebuilding a program from documentation and black - box observations . It supplements the benchmark rules ; it never permits source retrieval , internet access , decompilation , tracing , or reuse of the reference executable . ## Evidence - first workflow 1. Read all bundled documentation and turn it into a compact behavior ledger : commands , flags , inputs , outputs , exit status , file effects , defaults , error behavior , formatting , and explicitly documented edge cases . 2. Establish a runnable skeleton early . Create ‘ compile . sh ’, build a minimal independent executable , and confirm the complete build / run cycle before investing in secondary behavior . 3. Probe the reference through its normal public interface . Use small , discriminating experiments that separate plausible behaviors ; record the observed input , output , status , and state change instead of relying on assumptions based on the program name . 4. Prioritize breadth before polish . Implement the documented happy paths and common input classes , then error handling , boundary cases , formatting , and low - frequency options . Keep a list of remaining unsupported behavior . 5. Compare your implementation and the reference on the same locally generated cases . When they differ , reduce the case and fix the underlying general rule rather than adding a one - off special case . 6. Rebuild from a clean state periodically . A solution that works only because of cached artifacts , undeclared tools , or files outside the submission is not complete . 7. Before finalizing , verify that ‘ compile . sh ’ is executable , produces ‘./ executable ’ without network access , and that representative success and failure probes agree with the reference . ## Efficiency rules - Batch independent documentation reads and related probes when practical . - Prefer high - information probes over broad random exploration . - Keep outputs bounded and summarize findings in the behavior ledger . - Stop repeating probes once a stable rule has been established . - Reserve the final portion of the budget for a clean rebuild and end - to - end validation rather than continued exploration . ## Reference lifecycle Keep the black - box reference available until differential validation is finished . Develop a separately built candidate at another path , with the same executable basename where relevant . Do not overwrite the reference during implementation . If a permitted move is necessary , retain the execute - only reference on the same filesystem without reading / copying its bytes or changing its permissions . The reference is only a development oracle : never include it in the submission or invoke it from the submitted implementation . Vicky Zhao Affiliation: Tsinghua University Jie Tang Affiliation: Tsinghua University Abstract Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents. Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self-improvement (RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution costs. We introduce HarnessPro , a label-free method for evolving harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost. In this setting, candidate harnesses are evaluated using LLM-generated tests without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests. Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with different performance-cost priorities, and implement them as candidate harnesses. Rather than returning a single harness, HarnessPro uses normalized weighted squared-distance selection to provide cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) harnesses for different deployment budgets. Selected harnesses enter the next iteration, where execution feedback guides further updates. Our experiments cover Terminal-Bench 2, SWE-Bench Pro, and ProgramBench, using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Across these benchmarks using GPT-5.5 with Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro achieves an average pass-rate gain of 2.0 percentage points and an average per-task cost reduction of 26.1% relative to RHO. This advantage also holds when using GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Code is available at this link . 1 Introduction An agent harness is the software infrastructure that manages interactions between a large language model (LLM) and its environment ( Grace et al., 2026 ) . Recent work on recursive self-improvement (RSI) ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) uses past execution trajectories to diagnose problems and guide harness updates that improve performance on future tasks ( Suzgun et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ; Pan et al., 2026a ) . However, these methods often pursue performance gains through more extensive exploration and stronger verification ( Lin et al., 2026 ; Pan et al., 2026a ) . These efforts improve performance, but often at the cost of higher token consumption and increased latency. This trade-off is less appealing in practical deployment, where the execution cost and latency also matter. We therefore ask: Can recursive harness self-improvement deliver better performance at lower execution cost? Toward this goal, we introduce HarnessPro , a label-free method for recursive harness self-improvement that uses both performance and cost metrics to guide harness updates and candidate selection. It orchestrates several specialized agents to turn execution feedback into successive harness updates. A trajectory analyzer examines repeated rollouts to identify failures and avoidable overhead. Guided by different performance-cost priorities , a planner turns these diagnoses into harness improvement plans, which an editor implements as executable harness candidates. A test-synthesis agent provides fixed tests for evaluating the candidates without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests. Candidates that underperform the initial harness or are Pareto-dominated are discarded. To accommodate different budgets, we then use normalized weighted squared-distance selection ( Marler and Arora, 2004 ) to retain representative harnesses for cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) modes. The selected harnesses then enter the next epoch, where further updates pursue different performance-cost priorities. We evaluate HarnessPro on Terminal-Bench 2 ( The Terminal-Bench Team, 2025 ) , SWE-Bench Pro ( Deng et al., 2026 ) , and ProgramBench ( Yang et al., 2026a ) , using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. With both backbone models, HarnessPro improves task performance while reducing execution cost . For example, on Terminal-Bench 2 with GPT-5.5 and Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro outperforms RHO ( Pan et al., 2026a ) in pass rate by 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean cost per task by 33.9%. For more cost-sensitive deployments, the medium mode delivers performance comparable to RHO at substantially lower execution cost. An analysis of the evolved harnesses shows that HarnessPro does not improve agents simply by compressing context or increasing reasoning effort. The evolved harnesses dynamically allocate reasoning effort and tool budgets based on task descriptions, while runtime hooks steer execution from exploration toward convergence based on the assigned budgets. They also adopt tool-output compression like RTK ( Szymkowiak, 2026 ) and streamline instructions to reduce redundant prompt content, while retaining necessary context and final verification. Together, these mechanisms curb avoidable overhead while preserving the reasoning and verification needed for task success, thereby advancing the performance-cost Pareto frontier. Our contributions are threefold: • We introduce HarnessPro , a multi-agent framework that simultaneously optimizes performance and cost by analyzing execution trajectories and recursively improving harnesses. • We assess candidate artifacts with fixed LLM-generated tests rather than direct LLM judgments, improving failure detection without access to official tests. • Across three benchmarks, HarnessPro improves performance while reducing cost and latency, yielding a series of harnesses with different performance-cost trade-offs. 2 Related Work Agent and harness optimization. Agent optimization has expanded from prompts and pre-defined workflows to the executable harness surrounding a model. AFlow searches graphs of model-invoking operators using execution feedback ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . More recent systems directly modify harness components: agentic harness engineering makes edits traceable ( Lin et al., 2026 ) , HarnessFix diagnoses failures before applying repairs ( Chen et al., 2026a ) , and HarnessX composes harnesses from typed primitives using trajectory evidence ( Chen et al., 2026b ) . RHO uses LLMs to evaluate and compare execution trajectories without ground-truth labels, guiding harness evolution toward higher task success ( Pan et al., 2026a ) . In contrast, our method, HarnessPro , optimizes both task success rate and monetary cost. Rather than returning a single harness, it produces a set of harnesses with different performance-cost trade-offs, organized into lite, medium, and heavy tiers. Component optimization and inference-time budget allocation. Some methods focus on specific components, such as skills or memory ( Pan et al., 2026b ) . SkillOpt optimizes skill documents ( Yang et al., 2026b ) , while SkillMOO and FRAMES incorporate cost or regression constraints into skill evolution ( Gong et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Dynamic Cheatsheet and ReasoningBank retain reusable strategies from past experience ( Suzgun et al., 2026 ; Ouyang et al., 2026 ) , while Sleep-time Compute builds reusable memory by reasoning over context before a query arrives ( Lin et al., 2025 ) . MemoryCPT jointly optimizes memory construction, retrieval, and summarization ( Lei et al., 2026 ) . Other work addresses budget allocation at inference time: BATS learns a budget-aware policy for allocating model tokens and external tool calls ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , while COMPAS jointly selects models, prompts, and decoding settings according to task difficulty ( Gong et al., 2026b ) . HarnessPro instead uses past trajectories to evolve the entire harness, including instructions, skills, tools, hooks, and verification rules. We seek the Pareto frontier and select three representative operating points: cost-focused ( lite ), balanced ( medium ), and performance-focused ( heavy ). However, finding these trade-offs poses two challenges. (1) A vast harness search space. A harness comprises components such as instructions, tools, skills, hooks, and rules, all of which can be modified during evolution. Their possible combinations create a vast, discrete search space that cannot be optimized using gradients. (2) Balancing performance and cost. Additional reasoning, exploration, or verification can improve performance but also consumes more tokens, increasing cost. Conversely, indiscriminately reducing these activities may hurt performance. Advancing the Pareto frontier thus requires analyzing execution trajectories alongside task outcomes and token usage to distinguish necessary computation from avoidable overhead and find the “sweet spot” that reduces cost without compromising performance. 4 HarnessPro Figure 1: Overview of HarnessPro . In each epoch, it analyzes rollout trajectories, generates candidate harnesses, and selects representatives based on performance and cost. To address these challenges, we introduce HarnessPro , a multi-agent framework that analyzes execution trajectories and iteratively modifies harnesses to advance the performance-cost Pareto frontier. We first outline the evolution process, then describe trajectory-based diagnosis and candidate generation, followed by test-based evaluation and selection. 4.1 Overview To keep trajectory collection and analysis manageable, we begin by selecting a training coreset 𝒟 train \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} . Following RHO ( Pan et al., 2026a ) , we use the Determinantal Point Process (DPP) kernel ( Kulesza and Taskar, 2012 ) to balance task difficulty and diversity (Appendix A.1 ). On Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-Bench Pro, they select an execution profile from each task description. Each profile specifies a reasoning effort level and a tool-call budget. The lite, medium, and heavy modes use different rubrics for profile selection. Runtime hooks enforce the selected budget. For example, on Terminal-Bench 2, when HarnessPro -Medium selects the standard profile, the hooks remind the agent to produce parallel tool calls and avoid redundant checks after 14 tool calls, focus on completing and verifying the task after 26, and block further calls after 44. The reminders are appended to tool results, preserving the prompt prefix for cache reuse. Alongside these dynamic mechanisms, the evolved harnesses also reduce static context redundancy . On Terminal-Bench 2, for instance, tool-output compression like RTK ( Szymkowiak, 2026 ) folds repeated logs and condenses long outputs, while streamlined developer instructions reduce redundant input. This combination curbs recurring prompt overhead and limits the context growth caused by verbose tool feedback, thereby reducing execution cost and latency. To this end, it coordinates trajectory diagnosis and harness modification through a multi-agent framework, with a dedicated planner proposing update plans and LLM-generated tests guiding candidate evaluation. Rather than producing a single harness, HarnessPro offers cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) alternatives to meet different deployment budgets. Experiments across three benchmarks show that HarnessPro can improve task performance while reducing execution cost , with additional benefits in latency . Further analysis attributes these gains to the synergy of multiple evolved mechanisms and shows sustained progress through recursive self-improvement. These findings show that performance and efficiency can improve together, making cost-aware evolution a promising direction for practical recursive self-improvement in harness optimization. Seek genuine efficiency gains , not lower bills obtained by skipping required work , abandoning difficult tasks , or weakening validation . Use the diagnostics , trajectories , and candidate implementations to distinguish necessary work from avoidable expense . Look for recurring sources of redundant exploration , repeated context , or low - value verification . Consider the total cost of execution , including unsuccessful attempts and any overhead introduced by the proposed change ; fewer steps or shorter outputs alone do not establish an improvement . Possible directions include adapting reasoning effort to individual public tasks , managing context and tool feedback economically , and improving convergence or recovery . Preserve the information and checks needed for dependable results . These are optional search directions , not a checklist : derive any mechanism from the available evidence , without assuming a routing rubric , fixed thresholds , profile taxonomy , or per - task rules . Propose a focused , generalizable plan rather than accumulating optimizations . Explain which observed expense each change addresses , why correctness should be preserved , and what regression risks remain . Distinguish expected savings from measured results ; the fixed external evaluator , not the plan ’ s claims , determines whether quality is maintained and cost is reduced . ⬇ Seek a balanced improvement in task reliability and average execution cost . Treat correctness and efficiency as joint objectives : do not pursue savings by neglecting required behavior , or assume that additional computation necessarily improves quality . A balanced plan should improve the trade - off , not simply average the other directions . Use the diagnostics , trajectories , and candidate implementations to identify where effort contributes to successful completion and where it is redundant . Compare peer candidates to understand their strengths , weaknesses , and interactions , rather than copying their mechanisms wholesale . Prefer changes that remove low - value work while preserving or strengthening the reasoning and validation that matter . Possible directions include task - adaptive reasoning effort , concise but recoverable context , effective use of tool feedback , and verification or recovery guided by observed uncertainty . These are optional hypotheses , not prescribed designs . Infer an appropriate approach from the evidence ; no routing rubric , fixed thresholds , profile names , or per - task rules are supplied . Account for the overhead and complexity of combining changes . Propose a coherent , generalizable plan and explain its expected quality and cost effects together . Make uncertain trade - offs and regression risks explicit , including why any added work is worthwhile . Keep predicted benefits separate from established findings and let the fixed external evaluator determine whether the joint improvement is real . ⬇ Prioritize improving task success while continuing to eliminate avoidable expense . Focus on reliable completion and correct behavior , not more elaborate execution for its own sake . Performance - focused evolution should invest effort where it can address meaningful failures , rather than increase computation uniformly across tasks . Use the diagnostics , trajectories , and candidate implementations to identify consequential failure patterns and the limitations behind them . Examine both successful and unsuccessful executions to distinguish useful reasoning or validation from activity that merely adds cost . Draw on peer candidates when their behavior provides relevant evidence , but do not assume that a more complex harness is a more capable one . Possible directions include adapting reasoning effort to the public task , selective deeper investigation or independent verification , and stronger context or recovery management . These are optional hypotheses , not an implementation recipe . Derive the actual design from evidence ; no routing rubric , fixed thresholds , mandatory review schedule , or per - task rules are supplied . Preserve efficient behavior where additional work has no demonstrated purpose . Propose a focused , generalizable plan that explains which failures it aims to prevent and why the changes should help . If additional work is necessary , state the expected quality benefit , cost implications , and remaining risks without presenting predictions as measured gains . The fixed external evaluator determines whether the improvement justifies the resulting quality - cost trade - off .
